utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm sorry you've been kept waiting. There was a apparently some problem about the transport from the Detention Unit. Now, would you like to take the solemn declaration. If you'd like to stand to do it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you'd like to take a seat. Yes, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Madam, is your name Aferdita Hajrizi?

utterances.speaker: AFERDITA HAJRIZI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Were you born on the 29th of June, 1964?

utterances.speaker: AFERDITA HAJRIZI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Were you born in the village of Peran, in the municipality of Podujevo, in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: AFERDITA HAJRIZI
utterances.text: Yes. Now it's called Besiana municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Ms. Hajrizi, on the 3rd of June, 1999, did you provide a statement to representatives of the Office of the Prosecutor about events that you witnessed and experienced in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: AFERDITA HAJRIZI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And on the 20th of August, 2001, did you provide an additional statement to representatives of the Office of the Prosecutor about events that you witnessed and experienced in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: AFERDITA HAJRIZI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: On the 31st of January of this year, 2002, in the town of Mitrovica in Kosovo, were you provided with a copy of the statement that you made on the 3rd of June, 1999, in the presence of representatives of the Office of the Prosecutor and a presiding officer appointed by the Registrar of this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: AFERDITA HAJRIZI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Did you confirm at that time that the copy of the statement that you had made on 3 June 1999 was true and correct?

utterances.speaker: AFERDITA HAJRIZI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And on the 9th of March of this year, in the town of Mitrovica, Kosovo, were you provided with a copy of the statement that you made on the 20th of August, 2001, in the presence of representatives of the Office of the Prosecutor and a presiding officer appointed by the Registrar of this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: AFERDITA HAJRIZI
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And on that day, did you confirm that the copy of the statement that you made on the 20th of August, 2001 was true and correct?

utterances.speaker: AFERDITA HAJRIZI
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would now like to tender these two statements into evidence under Rule 92 bis.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This will be Exhibit 115, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honours, Aferdita Hajrizi grew up in the town of Mitrovica in Kosovo and received a degree in Albanian language and literature from Pristina University. Her late husband, Agim Hajrizi, was an activist on behalf of the rights of Kosovo Albanians and was the chairman of the Independent Kosovo Trade Union Assembly. Ms. Hajrizi's statements describe the harassment and threats directed at her family by Serb officials prior to the commencement of the international armed conflict in 1999. Ms. Hajrizi also describes the events of the evening of 24 March 1999, when Serb police broke into her family's home and shot to death her husband, Agim; her oldest son Ilir, who was then 11 years old; and her mother-in-law. During the next few days, Ms. Hajrizi and her surviving children hid in the Tavnik neighbourhood of Mitrovica until Serb forces began to burn homes and expel Kosovo Albanians from that neighbourhood on the 28th of March, 1999. Ms. Hajrizi and her family then joined a column of people and fled to the village of Zhabar. After three days in the village of Zhabar, Serb forces forced the Kosovo Albanians in that village to return to the town of Mitrovica. After several days in the town of Mitrovica, Ms. Hajrizi and her relatives boarded buses that Serb authorities had arranged to transport Kosovo Albanians to Montenegro. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, have you any questions for this witness?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mrs. Hajrizi, in view of this immense tragic loss that befell you, I shall restrict my questions to very few. The most necessary ones only, really. In your statement, on page 3, in paragraphs 3 and 4, you say -- actually, I'm just going to read out a small section. "It took me about ten minutes to reach the meeting point." This took place after this tragic event. You went to -- well, you say, anyway: "It took me about 10 minutes to reach the meeting point. The Serb soldiers did not harm me, but sometimes I had to wait and hide to let them pass." This is already your feeling, but the core of the matter is: "The Serb soldiers did not harm me." In the next paragraph, you speak about your brother who came to pick you up in his taxi, and towards the end of this paragraph, you say: "About ten metres away --" this is approximately the distance between you and me now. "About ten metres away, there were some policemen, but they did not harm us." So the soldiers and the policemen, according to your own description, behaved normally. None of them did you any harm. And according to the description of events that you gave - because it's tragic; you lost your son, your husband, your mother-in-law - is it clear that this was done by criminals, that this was not done by any military or police unit?

utterances.speaker: AFERDITA HAJRIZI
utterances.text: Your first question is not clear to me. Can you please repeat it? And then I will answer about the other question, about taking -- me taking ten minutes. I'm not clear what you want to get -- where you want to get at.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That is not important. I was quoting the text of your statement. I can skip that sentence altogether. That's the way the paragraph starts, so I read it in order to identify the paragraph. The point is, "The Serb soldiers did not harm me." That is what it says in the third paragraph. And in the fourth paragraph, it says: "About ten metres away, there were some policemen, but they did not harm us." So here you speak both about soldiers and about policemen who did not harm you at all. Bearing that in mind, since I assume --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Just to be sure that this is clear for the witness, Mr. Milosevic is referring to the witness's second statement from --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Let's try and deal with it this way so that the witness can follow. Just one moment. What is being suggested, as I understand it, is this: Is that the soldiers and police did not harm you when you were leaving the scene. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What the accused is saying, that is utopia. The fact that we were harassed and attacked in our own home, as innocent citizens we were, the fact that a child, only 11-year-old, an old woman, 65 years old, who had done nobody any harm and was not responsible for what happened in Kosova, for the genocide perpetrated against our people, that shows that Serb police did not come there to save us, to spare us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let me interrupt. The point that is made, whether you agree with it or not, is that in the statement, it says that they didn't harm you. This was after the murders which had taken place. And what is suggested to you - and perhaps this is the point of the question - is that this was not a police or a military unit which committed the murders. What is being said and suggested is that it was criminals of some sort who did it. Now, can you identify those who were responsible for the murders? Can you say who they were?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. In my full responsibility, I can identify the perpetrators, because ten minutes before the crime was committed, my husband recognised them very well, because we saw in front of our door two black vehicles parked, and we saw six offspring of Milosevic inside the cars. Two were at the wheel and six others came out in the yard. My husband recognised four of them: Nenad Pavicevic, our neighbour, next-door neighbour, then Dejan, Boban, and Ratko Antonijevic. These four people my husband recognised, whereas the two others he did not. Two of them I know very well. As to Dejan and Ratko, I don't know them, even if I happened to see them today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You mentioned four people: Pavicevic, Dejan, and Boban [sic]. What were those people? What did they do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Pavicevic was the son of Dragica. He was a fatherless son, someone I used to know as of 1979, when he was a young boy. I knew them very well because I lived in that neighbourhood and in that house for 15 years in succession. And I know pretty well who they were and what mentality they had because we were neighbours and they passed by us and didn't greet us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Can you help us with this: What was their occupation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] His mother was a saleswoman. She worked in a store in Mitrovica. The mother of Pavicevic, Dragica, was a saleswoman, whereas Nenad was a student in the high school. After graduation from the high school, all those Serbs who couldn't find a job and who didn't have anything better to do, then they were recruited in the Serb police, with the sole destination of committing crimes against the innocent Albanian people, and he was -- Nenad Pavicevic was one of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And the others that you've mentioned, what were they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The other, Boban, I didn't know him very well until my husband showed me who he was. Lately - that is, in the last two, three years - he was engaged in criminal activity. Boban was a right-hand of Nenad. I have seen with my own eyes, in the middle of the marketplace, they were maltreating Albanians, imprisoning them. They were always active in such activities. Even the young children in Mitrovica know Nenad and Boban. As I said, I didn't know him personally as well as I did Nenad, who was my neighbour, but seeing what they did every day to Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. the Albanians -- I saw from my own balcony them bringing out of the car, seeing things they looted from Albanians and bringing them home, to Nenad's home.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wish to have the facts clarified. In her statement, the witness described the events concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did I understand this correctly: What you described, the murder, the murder in your house, according to what you have been saying yourself, this was carried out by your neighbours. Is that right or is it not right?

utterances.speaker: AFERDITA HAJRIZI
utterances.text: Yes. My neighbour, together with seven other criminals. They were accomplices, under the orders of the accused. I think they acted on orders coming from their superiors.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. We are not going into that now, what the opinion may be. I wish to establish the facts. You confirmed that this was committed by your neighbours along with a few other criminals, as you have been saying. That is obviously what I asked you. And I asked you whether you are aware of the fact that this was not done by any police or military unit but that it was done by criminals.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The witness has answered the question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In your statement, in your statement when you mention the -- when you mention a police unit or an army unit, you mention them later in the street and in the contacts you had with your brother. You say that neither the soldiers nor the policemen did you any harm. Is that right or is that not right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We've been through this too.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please, Your Honours. If I may. Nenad Pavicevic was a policeman at that time when the crime was committed in my very home. The accused cannot say that the police have not done such things because this was done in cooperation with the Serb police and other criminals who subscribed to that crime. It's not true that the police have not done it. Nenad and Dejan, both of them were policemen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Hajrizi, do you perhaps know that both the police and the army, during this 78-day war, had orders and carried out their orders to arrest people who committed such crimes, including --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: This is not for the witness. She is describing what she saw and heard.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Now I have to ask her about things that I have received by way of information.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you this because in the report that I received from my associates, it says that policemen -- the policemen that you mentioned as responsible for the murders were at Gazivode on that day to meet the family of their killed colleague Marash at the border with Montenegro, and it says in that report that a great many of them were there, headed by their commander. Are you sure when you claim that it is precisely these people that you mentioned were at the same time in your house?

utterances.speaker: AFERDITA HAJRIZI
utterances.text: Your informers must have been very weak. They have sent you very inaccurate information. I am 100 per cent sure that those people were there in my home. I can prove this with what I saw. I saw in front of my house Nenad Pavicevic, whom I know for 20 years, and his friend Boban. And I keep saying that I saw Dejan and Ratko Antonijevic, whom I never know and don't know even today. So I'm still saying that you have wrong information. I can prove it also with the other fact that I was in the attic in my own home with my two surviving children, and I very clearly heard the voice of my mother-in-law telling him, "Nenad, how can you kill my son?" You can ask me whether they were masked. I can tell you very well that these people standing in front of my home, those six policemen, were not masked. They had black berets, and I could see their face very distinctly. We could identify all of them because the road was lit that night. Your informers have told you where my house is located. It is located in the centre of the town. Across our house, there are some stores and they were very well lit that night. And from where I stood in the window, I could see very well who they were. So I'm reiterating that you have wrong information.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I was just seeking for an answer to my question, and I have received it. Now, were you present on the following day when the investigating judge by the name of Vesna Ristic, a lady, went out to the scene of the crime and conducted an investigation with respect to the killing? From the information that I received yesterday, it says here that the investigating judge, Vesna Ristic, went out to the crime scene. She was accompanied by an Albanian doctor. And it also says that this man Pavicevic went out too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the witness deal with this first of all. Were you present when the investigating judge came to the house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Next question. She wasn't present, so she can't help with that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, do you know that afterwards, during the investigation, a large number of casings were found, 7.62 calibre, produced by China, and two 5.65 casings from these pistols? Did anybody give you a report that was written by the investigating judge?

utterances.speaker: AFERDITA HAJRIZI
utterances.text: When were the -- where were these weapons found, Accused?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just deal with the questions, please. We'll get on more quickly. Did you get the report or any report from any investigating judge?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, never.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Next question, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that this incident was reported by your uncle, or perhaps your husband's uncle, Pllana, to the president of the district court? "M. Ivanovic" the name given here is. Is that how the crime was reported, in fact?

utterances.speaker: AFERDITA HAJRIZI
utterances.text: You've erroneous information. Pllana is not my -- is the son of my aunt, Skender Pllana, who on the next day -- he was -- donned a uniform, and on the next day he put on another uniform. And as of 8.00 in the morning, he kept patrolling in front of the door of our home when the investigating judge came and asked for some relative of the family to go inside and identify the corpses. That means to go inside for the third time: The first time when the crime was committed; second time in the middle of the night when Nenad Pavicevic entered and looted all the valuable things he found in my home. He stole all the documents that you needed, as your power needed. And the third time when he changed the uniform and patrolled in the front of the door in the hope that I would show up. And when the judge asked, "Who is the closest relative to this family who wishes to identify the bodies?" Skender Pllana showed up and said, "I am the one." At that moment, Nenad Pavicevic responded, "Why are you coming and pretending you are the closest relative? Where is Aferdita and the two children? I want her to come here, because Agim Hajrizi has also two other children, and we want to kill them too." This is the truth, distinguished -- Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't want to go into whether it was your uncle or the uncle's son, but he was present during the investigation that was carried out. Now I have another question to ask you in that regard. This investigation, is it conducted by the district court in Mitrovica today? Is it an ongoing process? Are proceedings under way today?

utterances.speaker: AFERDITA HAJRIZI
utterances.text: Everything that the Mitrovica District Court did were mere formality, because the judge of Mitrovica court was very well informed, as the accused knows very well, that none of this happened by accident in my home, and they merely came to carry out the formalities. Because they knew very well who was going to be killed that night, who was going to be killed. The two most distinguished activists of Mitrovica were killed. They worked for the benefit of their people and for working people, and they never did any harm to anybody. So the judge carried out the most minimal formalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I don't think you understood my question. I was asking you about now. Are proceedings, legal proceedings, under way now in connection with this murder, and are they being conducted in the district court in Kosovska Mitrovica?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Can you help us with that? Fairly briefly, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understood the question very well, and I gave a very good answer to the first question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. Just tell us: Do you know -- you may not know, but do you know if there are investigations continuing or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In August 2000, I was present at the judgement of Lazar Gligorovski and Nenad Pavicevic, who was in absentia. After two hours and a half of statement, I said, and I say again, that the assassination that Gligorovski committed against my family, at which my father-in-law and Agim were present, he tried to commit -- to murder us, and the police came, after three hours, came to Lazar Gligorovski's house and said to him clearly, "When did you use your gun? Why didn't you carry out your duty?" I was present during that trial process in 2000, and I was there, and according to the Swedish prosecutor who was present in the trial, Lazar Gligorovski was declared innocent, whereas Nenad Pavicevic was sentenced to 20 years of prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That's why I asked you: Were legal proceedings undertaken at the district court in Kosovska Mitrovica?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And have any other proceedings been undertaken in respect of any of the other persons who were involved in this murder?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: They can't hear you. They can't hear you. Have you got your microphone on?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Somebody switched it off. I hope you can hear now. Can you hear me now? Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In the statement given on the 3rd of June, 1999, describing the first day of the NATO bombing, you say that you took your family to a shelter underneath the staircase that had been prepared previously. Now, when did you prepare this shelter that you mention in your statement?

utterances.speaker: AFERDITA HAJRIZI
utterances.text: I didn't say that we went to a place of shelter. We stayed in our Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. own home and we made a shelter under the steps of our house, under the steps of the first floor. We didn't go anywhere. We were in our own home.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I didn't say that you went anywhere. I was just reading what you said in your own statement, and I read out the following sentence: "I took my family to the shelter underneath the steps," or stairway.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What page are we dealing with, Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In my version, it is on page 5, paragraph 1; page 5, line 7. And it says: "I took my family to a shelter underneath the staircase which we had prepared beforehand."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: My question was: When did you prepare this shelter that you mentioned in your statement? And you mentioned it once again just now.

utterances.speaker: AFERDITA HAJRIZI
utterances.text: I will tell you what kind of shelter I had. My son, Ilir, took a carpet from the room which we had spare and spread it out, because, as a child, he was rather frightened and he thought that he would be safer under the stairs. And it consisted of a few pieces of wood, which enabled the children to go under the stairs of the first floor. That's the shelter that I was talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I didn't understand you to be talking about that, because you wrote "shelter" here. Mrs. Hajrizi, you're an intellectual. Your husband was an intellectual as well. Are you conscious of the fact of who pushed the citizens of Kosovo into the war and into all these tragic events that followed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. This is not a matter for the witness. It's a matter which this Trial Chamber is going to have to determine.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Very well, Mr. May. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If I can ask you some questions about one matter, and that concerns Nenad Pavicevic. He was a neighbour of yours; is that right?

utterances.speaker: AFERDITA HAJRIZI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: His mother lived in the house next door to your family; is that right?

utterances.speaker: AFERDITA HAJRIZI
utterances.text: We were only separated by one wall.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And his family had lived there for many years; is that right?

utterances.speaker: AFERDITA HAJRIZI
utterances.text: My husband's family came a hundred years ago, and they know very well where they come from. They've been living for many years in ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did the mother of Nenad Pavicevic not have friendly relations with your family?

utterances.speaker: AFERDITA HAJRIZI
utterances.text: We never had bad relations or good relations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did his mother throw rubbish and medicines into your family compound?

utterances.speaker: AFERDITA HAJRIZI
utterances.text: No. Nenad's mother, no. But Dragica, Nenad's mother, taught her 5- or 6-year-old son, as my mother-in-law told me. I wasn't married at this time. But this child threw medicines in the well in my yard, from which well our family drank water.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And was that Nenad Pavicevic?

utterances.speaker: AFERDITA HAJRIZI
utterances.text: Yes. Nenad Pavicevic, his mother.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So from the ages of a small child, Nenad Pavicevic was causing trouble to your family; is that right?

utterances.speaker: AFERDITA HAJRIZI
utterances.text: A person, to become a criminal and to commit crimes like he did, he has to have a mother like this. Because we have a proverb: Where does a child's education begin? A child's education begins 20 years before he is born. To have a well-brought-up child, you have to have well-brought-up parents, and this man comes from a family with natural criminal tendencies. A mother with criminal tendencies brings forth a child of this kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So it would be right to say that Nenad Pavicevic, as a neighbour to you, had bad relations with your family and caused your family trouble?

utterances.speaker: AFERDITA HAJRIZI
utterances.text: I cannot -- may I continue? I can't say this. We never -- we never interfered with their business and never provoked them in any way. Beforehand, we had never had any family problems. This was the way they were brought up. They didn't speak to their neighbours. They didn't greet them. But we never had any conflict between our families.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Ms. Hajrizi, I have a few questions for you. I'd like you to please try to keep your responses short, if you can, so we can move along as efficiently as possible. Just to clarify some points that Mr. Kay was making. Mr. Kay asked you whether Nenad Pavicevic lived next door to your family, and your response was yes, but I need you to clarify which family; the family home that you shared with your husband and your children, or the family home that your husband grew up in before he married out and where your mother-in-law lived before she died?

utterances.speaker: AFERDITA HAJRIZI
utterances.text: Please, I didn't understand the question. If you could repeat it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Kay asked you whether Nenad Pavicevic and his mother lived next door to your family, and your response was yes. However --

utterances.speaker: AFERDITA HAJRIZI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: -- when you describe -- when you say that Mr. Pavicevic and his mother lived next door to your family, are you referring to the home that you shared with your husband and your children, or are you referring to your husband's -- the home of your husband's extended family and the home that he grew up in?

utterances.speaker: AFERDITA HAJRIZI
utterances.text: I'm talking about the house in which my husband and I lived.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. And you mentioned that Mr. Nenad Pavicevic, even as a child, would throw inappropriate things into the family's well; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AFERDITA HAJRIZI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Or as Mr. Kay put it, he was causing trouble to your family, right?

utterances.speaker: AFERDITA HAJRIZI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And then when this young man grew up and finished school, he was then employed by the Serb police; is that right?

utterances.speaker: AFERDITA HAJRIZI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Let's talk a bit about the night when your husband, your son, and your mother-in-law were killed. You mentioned that there was a man named Boban there who was present with Nenad. Did the man that you knew as Boban -- was he also a policeman?

utterances.speaker: AFERDITA HAJRIZI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And before the -- and before the killings occurred that evening, did you also see the man that you knew as Boban standing outside your home by the two cars?

utterances.speaker: AFERDITA HAJRIZI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: In response to one of the questions that you were asked, you said that the two most distinguished activists in Mitrovica were killed on that night. Now, your husband was killed just after the NATO bombing began; is that right?

utterances.speaker: AFERDITA HAJRIZI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: It was on the evening of the 24th of March or the early morning of the 25th of March, 1999?

utterances.speaker: AFERDITA HAJRIZI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Besides your husband - and I'm going to come back to him in a minute - who was the other distinguished activist in Mitrovica who was killed that night?

utterances.speaker: AFERDITA HAJRIZI
utterances.text: The other Mitrovica activist who was killed on the same night was the honoured teacher Latif Berisha, who at that time was chairman of the Kosova Democratic League for the Mitrovica branch.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And how far did Mr. Berisha live from your home?

utterances.speaker: AFERDITA HAJRIZI
utterances.text: I can say about -- it's in the same direction as our house but divided by the river Ibar. He lived in the village of Suhodoll, not far from the town of Mitrovica, rather, in the outskirts of the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can you give an estimate in hundreds of metres or in kilometres?

utterances.speaker: AFERDITA HAJRIZI
utterances.text: I wouldn't say no more than two kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Before your husband, Agim Hajrizi, was killed that night, what was his occupation?

utterances.speaker: AFERDITA HAJRIZI
utterances.text: My husband's profession was -- in 1985, he was employed by the battery factory in Mitrovica as head of the computer department in this factory. In 1989, all the Albanians were dismissed en masse from their jobs. They were dismissed by the Serbian regime of the accused, the Milosevic regime. After 1989, hunger came. There was a very difficult social situation in our city, because Mitrovica is an industrial city. It lives from industry. But all the factories were closed and people had no way of making a livelihood.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Saxon. We need to move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Prior to the night he was killed, what was your husband doing for a living? How did he spend his time? In 1998 and the first part of 1999.

utterances.speaker: AFERDITA HAJRIZI
utterances.text: In 1998/1999, my husband was at the head of the assembly of the independent trade unions of Kosova. So in the service of the working class and the poorer layers of the Albanian population.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And my last question: Prior to the night he was killed, how many times, approximately, had your husband been detained by Serb authorities?

utterances.speaker: AFERDITA HAJRIZI
utterances.text: There were any number of occasions. I wouldn't be able to count them. Many, many times he was taken from his home. He was taken on the street. He was beaten, mistreated, kept in prison for up to 18 hours. He was mistreated in front of his own children. There was a particular case in August 1998 when, together with my young son Arianiti, who at that time was five years old, about one kilometre from home, four police vehicles lead by Nenad Pavicevic stopped my husband. They arrested him and told him to fetch -- to put his five-year-old child in the police car too. But because he refused, my child was left in the middle of the road to the mercy of fate. My husband was arrested, and my terrified child returned home alone and said to me, "Mommy, Nenad took Daddy." That is one case, but there were many cases in which he was arrested and mistreated.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Saxon, I wonder if the Prosecution could present the Court in due course the judgement referred to by Mrs. Hajrizi today as having been entered against Nenad Pavicevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Yes. We will undertake to do that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I would appreciate it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mrs. Hajrizi, help us with this if you would: Going back to the night of the murders --

utterances.speaker: AFERDITA HAJRIZI
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: -- you said that the lights in the street were on; is that right?

utterances.speaker: AFERDITA HAJRIZI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And also, is it right that there were shops opposite you which were still lit?

utterances.speaker: AFERDITA HAJRIZI
utterances.text: Quite correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You said the men were not masked, and they had on black berets.

utterances.speaker: AFERDITA HAJRIZI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Could you tell us if they were wearing uniform or not, or what they were wearing.

utterances.speaker: AFERDITA HAJRIZI
utterances.text: Yes. They were uniformed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And what was the uniform?

utterances.speaker: AFERDITA HAJRIZI
utterances.text: The uniform was dark blue and camouflage patterned, with black berets on their heads.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you for coming to the International Tribunal to give your evidence, Mrs. Hajrizi. You are free to go.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We can't hear. Your microphone.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm interested in knowing what this subsequent examination of the witness means on the part of the Prosecution, an examination which has nothing to do with my cross-examination. Does that mean that after my cross-examination, he is continuing his examination-in-chief, which he does not wish to conduct because of the specific treatment that these statements have?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The rule is that the Prosecution have the right, as always, of re-examination, and they're entitled to re-examine a witness after your cross-examination. Your cross-examination was directed to showing that those involved in the murders were criminals. The re-examination was directed to showing that the husband of the witness who was murdered had been an activist and that an activist was also murdered, another activist was also murdered on the same night. That is relevant. It will be a matter for us to consider in due course. So the answer is that the Prosecution are entitled to re-examine on matters arising out of cross-examination and can ask relevant questions in relation to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. The next witness, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. The Prosecution calls Mehmet Aliu.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I should say we'll sit until shortly after eleven. We'll take one break and then go on until about 1.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't know whether the brief skeleton summary has been distributed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. We will have it in due course. Yes. Let the witness take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you'd like to take a seat.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Aliu, do I understand correctly, sir, that you are, at the moment, 56 years old?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET ALIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And you are of the Muslim religion and of ethnic Albanian background; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET ALIU
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Sir, where do you live or where did you live in March of 1999?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET ALIU
utterances.text: I lived in Prishtina, in Kodra e Trimave neighbourhood.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And is it -- are you married, sir?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET ALIU
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And how many children do you have?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET ALIU
utterances.text: I have six children of my own plus another adopted one.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And what is your occupation, sir?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET ALIU
utterances.text: I am a construction worker.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And do I understand, sir, you've been self-employed, owning your own business for the last 20 years or so?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET ALIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Now, sir, did there come a time when members of the Office of the Prosecutor attended on you and took a statement from you on the 3rd of July of 2001?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET ALIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And were you subsequently shown a translation of that statement in your language, the Albanian language --

utterances.speaker: MEHMET ALIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: -- on the 2nd of February, 2002?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET ALIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: In your statement you had also referred to some photographs and other documents; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET ALIU
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: When you saw this translation of your statement, did you appear before a Presiding Officer of this Court and swear that the contents of your -- or solemnly declare that the contents of your statement were true and accurate to the best of your knowledge and belief?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET ALIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Might that statement, with attachments, be marked as the next exhibit, please, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Now, Witness, you say that you come from Kodra e Trimave. Now, is that a village or is that an actual neighbourhood in Pristina?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET ALIU
utterances.text: It is a neighbourhood in Prishtina called Kodra e Trimave.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: So it is not a separate village on its own?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET ALIU
utterances.text: No, it is not.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Now, you come originally from the Podujevo municipality, do you, sir?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET ALIU
utterances.text: Yes, Hertica village, Podujevo municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And then you moved from Hertica to Pristina itself, in the Pristina municipality?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET ALIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. I may have moved too quickly before we actually had an exhibit number assigned to the statement with attachments.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. It's Exhibit 116.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, Your Honours, if it assists at all, Pristina can be found on Exhibit 83, map 7, and it's very clear where that is. It's the big yellow town. And Hertica is found on the same map, about halfway in the middle of the map, down from number 3, at the top. So 3 and 10. Those would be the coordinates. You see Hertica and Podujevo. If I may briefly outline, for the benefit of the wider audience, the highlights of this witness's statement. I propose to do that now. I understand, Your Honours, that in the statement that has been marked as the exhibit, the witness describes oppression of Albanians by the Serbs during the decade of the 1990s, including the exclusion of Albanians from schools. This led to home schools being set up, and one such home school was set up in the witness's home. The Serb police tried to close the school down on a number of occasions, and the witness describes how he, the school teachers, and the pupils were harassed by the Serb police, and refers to incidents when he was beaten. As a result of these incidents, the witness sent his immediate family, save for his wife, to Germany for safety. The witness also will describe for you in the statement that he joined the KLA in 1991 and that in the time immediately prior to the start of the NATO bombing, he was in fact in the hills around Podujevo with the KLA. He received information that Serb forces were expelling people from villages and towns around Pristina, and then on or about the 25th of March - now, this is a correction, I understand, from what is in the statement. His statement refers to the 28th of March - the witness returned to his home with nine other family members who were also associated with the KLA. Then I understand that on or about the 26th of March - not the 30th of March, as indicated in the statement - he saw Serb forces and police expelling Albanian civilians from Pristina. The area around his home and yard contained approximately 10.000 civilians from villages around Pristina, and the witness was requested by these civilians to assist in locating others who had been lost or killed or injured in and around the surrounding area. On the 28th of March, the witness saw Serb police pursuing civilians and shooting at them, and he says that 12 to 13 civilians, at least, to his knowledge, were shot dead. He describes how the police rounded up the civilians in a meadow, where they were forced to lie down, and they were later released and directed to go to the Pristina railway station by the police. He describes that the crowd of people in the witness's yard were terrified by what they had seen, and some of them left, but about 300 remained. The Serbs forces surrounded the neighbourhood, and the witness saw two men being killed by the police. The police then tried to force entry to the witness's yard, and other KLA members, including the witness, returned fire. Later that afternoon, two Serb tanks arrived and broke down the front gate, causing the KLA to retreat. His house was completely destroyed. That night the witness told the civilians to make their way to the railway station. My understanding is that the witness continued with his KLA activities until the end of the war. That is a very, very brief outline of this witness's evidence, to put the potential cross-examination into context. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your activities started, as you said, since your education, since school.

utterances.speaker: MEHMET ALIU
utterances.text: Underground.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You assert that Albanian children were expelled from schools.

utterances.speaker: MEHMET ALIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Why do you assert that when you know that's not true?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET ALIU
utterances.text: How can you say that is not true?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I can say it's not true because the facts speak otherwise. Do you know that your politicians ordered children to get out of schools because they did not want children to study according to programmes, curricula, that applied to all children in Serbia? Do you know that? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MEHMET ALIU
utterances.text: We know that in the 1990s, 1991, you started to change the curricula and not give them in Albanian, but only teach them in Serbian. It is true that our students didn't want to learn the Serb curricula. I can base it on my own arguments and on arguments provided by internationals.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So your pupils left schools because they did not want to study according to the Serbian school programme; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET ALIU
utterances.text: They were forcibly removed from school by the police and were prevented to enter their schools. In June 1991, when the students went to take their exams, the door of the school was closed by the police, and the police beat them, and they didn't let them enter the school, neither the students nor the professors. Protests were staged --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Try to make up your mind. What is the truth? Was the truth that they did not want to study according to the Serbian school programme, as you had put it, or is it true that they were forcibly thrown out of the schools? Is it one or the other?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET ALIU
utterances.text: The truth is that they left the school because they didn't want to learn in the Serb curricula, and your Serb military and police regime did not allow them to go back to school before they accepted to learn in the Serb language and with the Serb programmes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know that there is no special programme for Kosovo, that all the children in Serbia studied according to the same programme?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET ALIU
utterances.text: We know that we used to have our own programme. I myself learned with a programme of Kosova. But in 1991, these programmes were removed and you tried to force us to accept your Serb programmes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And why didn't it bother Hungarians to study according to these programmes that applied to all children, or Bulgarians or Slovaks or anybody else? It was only you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's not a matter for the witness to answer. You needn't bother to answer that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So the Albanians left the schools because they did not want to study according to the Serbian school programme, as you had put it. Do you know, do you know, that until the 23rd of March, 1999 -- or do you know how many pupils there were in your town in Pristina, how many attended state schools and studied in the Serb language and how many studied in the Albanian language?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET ALIU
utterances.text: I'm not clear about the question. Can you repeat it, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that children, Albanian children in Kosovo, all got their education in the Albanian language, all of the Albanian children who attended state schools?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET ALIU
utterances.text: Up to 1990, 1991, they have followed the state schools. As of June 1991 onwards, all the schools were closed down and the professors were fired, and they were imprisoned, maltreated, persecuted by the police. We have documents to prove it. If the Honourable Court wishes so, I can provide it with documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know that in that same spot where you're sitting now there were people who worked in schools with 1.200, 1.500, 1.800 pupils, and they confirmed that they worked --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, there's no point in putting that to the witness. He doesn't know what the other witnesses said. If there's a discrepancy, you can point it out in due course in argument, but there's no point in putting it to the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is no point because there is a difference between ignorance and falsehoods, Mr. May, and the difference is a big one at that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that in the municipality of Pristina, until the 23rd of March, 1999 - so I'm not talking about 1990 or 1991 - only in the municipality of Pristina there were 6.535 pupils studying in the Serb language? In the Serb language, 6.535. And in state schools -- there were 23.511 pupils studying in the Albanian language in state schools in the municipality where you live. Are you aware of these figures?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET ALIU
utterances.text: No, I'm not aware. And furthermore, that's not true. That number of students applies to those students that were taught in private homes. And it's true that teaching continued but in homes and in very difficult conditions. Often students were checked in buses, and they were searched whether they had Albanian books in their backpacks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: We heard that. But that's not what I'm asking you. I am asking you whether you know of any Albanian children who went to state schools after 1990; that is to say, 1993, 1995, 1996, 1997, 1998. Do you know of any who went to Albanian-speaking schools that were state schools?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET ALIU
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It is your assertion that Albanian children did not go to state schools?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET ALIU
utterances.text: They followed primary school up to the eighth year of school, but not the high schools or higher, the university.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Ah, now you've made a concession. Albanian children did attend primary schools.

utterances.speaker: MEHMET ALIU
utterances.text: Not a teacher, not a professor was paid by the state. All of them were paid by the funds put together by voluntary people. None of them worked for the state. They were not paid social insurance by the state.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That's not what I asked you. You are answering my questions now. Did Albanian children attend state schools, primary schools? Just say yes or no. That's what I'm asking you.

utterances.speaker: MEHMET ALIU
utterances.text: I told you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes or no. Did they go or did they not go?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET ALIU
utterances.text: No, they didn't go to state schools. They followed the lessons in those homes. Why did we allow them to have our facilities, home facilities if there were state facilities?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. All right. You've answered the question. You said yourself that it did not suit some. It did not suit you. The programme that was applied to all children in Serbia did not suit you. But because there were some who did find it suitable, some did go to school.

utterances.speaker: MEHMET ALIU
utterances.text: It's not true that I said so. I said that you have changed the curriculum. And by so doing, we didn't want to go to those schools and learn with those programmes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Which programme was changed, the curriculum with mathematics or biology?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET ALIU
utterances.text: Education -- the curriculum in general was changed, the educational programme. You forced us to speak Serbian as an official language in Kosova, and the curriculum suffered many changes. I can't tell you how many, but there were many. Considerable changes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did Albanian children receive their education in the Serb language or in the Albanian language?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET ALIU
utterances.text: In the Albanian language.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: According to law and according to the school programme, Albanian children studied in the Albanian language.

utterances.speaker: MEHMET ALIU
utterances.text: In the home school.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In the state schools too. I read the figures out to you awhile ago how many attended school in the Albanian language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The witness has disputed the figures. Now, we've -- just a moment. Just a moment. We've spent a very great deal of time on education already in this case, and we've already indicated our view that it is a peripheral issue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In this specific case, a great deal has to do with schools. And also, as you say, the witness disputed the figures. He did not only dispute the figures, he disputed the presence of Albanian children in schools at all, in general. He claims that Albanian children did not go to school at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. He's given an indication -- he's given an indication of where they went to school. Now, let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It is your assertion that you are a member of the KLA; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET ALIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When did you exactly become a member of the KLA?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET ALIU
utterances.text: That is my secret. I have no reason to tell you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Is there any particular reason why it's a secret? Is there any reason why you shouldn't tell us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's not a secret to you, but it is for him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, tell us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From the moment when the violence started in Kosova. From the moment when the Jashari family was massacred. Not only myself but the entire Albanian population mobilised, and they decided there was nothing -- no longer any life in Kosova unless we rose in an uprising. Are you satisfied with my answer?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Don't ask us that. But you're here to tell the truth, and I'm sure you will. Now -- just a moment. The Jashari family were massacred, you say. So that was in 1998 - we've heard the evidence about that - is that right? Fairly early in the year, as I recollect.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] March.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: We have heard in the summary that the opposing party presented that you became a member of the KLA in 1991. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET ALIU
utterances.text: The KLA started from March 1998 and continued until 1999, until the liberation of Kosova.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I said 1991 and typed 1991, that's an error. That's my fault.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It is in the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It is in the summary at the second paragraph, and the witness said that, "In around 1991, I did join the UCK."

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. That can be clarified. But I have copied from the statement, which I believe was a typo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We can clarify in due course when it was the KLA became operative.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is precisely what the question was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How could you become a member in 1991 when this terrorist KLA was organised much later?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He's given his answer about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And which way did you join the KLA? How did you join up?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET ALIU
utterances.text: I joined the KLA as a head of logistics, and I had the duty of supplying all the goods the KLA needed within the resources that we have. It wasn't just myself but a group of others.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But you were the chief person in charge of logistics. You were the chief of logistics. That's the way you put it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He's just said that. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what did that mean? What did that imply, setting the logistics of the KLA?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET ALIU
utterances.text: Supplies it involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Of what?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET ALIU
utterances.text: Everything that was needed. What I was able to supply, because there was a lot of needs but not all of them were possible to be met.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You said that you also did some intelligence matters with respect to the KLA around Pristina. Now, what kind of intelligence matters?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET ALIU
utterances.text: I don't know what you're implying by "spying."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm just thinking about what you yourself mentioned in your statement, so I assume that you know what you were thinking of when you wrote that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Read the passage from the statement so the witness can know what you're talking about.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll try and find it. I assumed that the witness would know what he said, so I didn't mark the passage in the statement itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The first page of the statement, second paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It says: "I was also able to supply information on intelligence matters as to what was occurring with the Serb police in and around Pristina." Yes. That is what it says in your statement.

utterances.speaker: MEHMET ALIU
utterances.text: When I was at the headquarters there, we watched Serbian police radio links, and I heard orders coming from Belgrade that all the villages around Prishtina, like Obiliq, Orlovic, Bardh i Madhe, as far as Vushtrria, all the villagers should be expelled in the direction of Prishtina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you're claiming that the policemen in Pristina, via radio link, were able to communicate with policemen in Belgrade; is that it?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET ALIU
utterances.text: Not with Belgrade, but Misko Lakovic said that orders had come from Belgrade that all the villagers around Prishtina, all the population, should be expelled in the direction of Prishtina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And who is Misko Lakovic?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET ALIU
utterances.text: No. He was an officer, a leading officer of the police for Prishtina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. We can return to this after the adjournment. Just a moment. We'll adjourn now until -- it's time for adjournment. We'll adjourn until half past 11.00. Mr. Aliu, during the adjournment, would you remember, please, not to speak to anybody about your evidence until it's over, and that includes the members of the Prosecution team.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please: In which way did you come by the information that would be interesting for the KLA?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Do you understand the question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not clear about the question. I don't know what he means by "information for the benefit of the KLA." I don't get it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know what is not clear in my question, but let me try and explain. You say you collected information for the KLA. Now, I'm asking you: How did you come by that information? How did you collect the information?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET ALIU
utterances.text: You said -- you used the word "information." I didn't say that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He's given an example of hearing something at the headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You said that you tried to listen in to the conversations that the police had in Lapastica, by Podujevo; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET ALIU
utterances.text: Yes, it is right that I heard that piece of information about the displacement of the population from the villages in the direction of the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, were these telephone conversations or did these conversations take place in another way?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET ALIU
utterances.text: I heard it on the radio, through the radio relay the police used.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. So you listened in to the conversations that the police had via radio. Is that what you're claiming? You intercepted them?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET ALIU
utterances.text: Yes, radio connection.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And I also understood a moment ago that you said that you had heard the chief of police issuing some sort of order through this radio link.

utterances.speaker: MEHMET ALIU
utterances.text: Through this radio link I heard him ordering the police stations of Obiliq, Fushe Kosove, to displace the entire population in the direction of Prishtina. This is what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Were those his words? Did he say it in just the way you have told us, or, from what I was able to understand, that he used codes to say what he wanted to say?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET ALIU
utterances.text: The order arrived from Belgrade for all the residents of the villages to be driven out of their homes and sent in the direction of Prishtina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. That's what you claim. But what did you actually hear? What did you actually hear this chief of police say, the one that you just mentioned?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET ALIU
utterances.text: I don't have here the recorded tape, but this is what I heard. I think I'm being clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But as far as I was able to understand you, you said that he used some codes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He didn't say "code."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you claim that through this relay station, he informed other police departments of orders allegedly received from Belgrade. Is that it?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET ALIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you hear --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a moment. Just a moment, Mr. Milosevic. Mr. Aliu, on page 5 of the English version, in your statement you said that, the first paragraph: "The order was to all the Serb forces that the Albanian civilians in the areas of," for example, "Fushe Kosove ... had to be been expelled. The conversation was in Serb. However, we were in possession of the codes that the Serbs were using for the names of the towns and villages." That's what you said in your earlier statement. So you were asked: What was the words exactly which you heard? And could you help us with the codes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I tried to explain that, through the radio link, we knew what codes they used for Prishtina, Obiliq, when they referred to these towns. So when they spoke to each other, communicated to each other on the radio, we knew what they were talking about. So when the order was issued, I realised that my house was in jeopardy. Because for many years I was the target of police attacks. I have even indicted the police who did that, the police of Milosevic's power, and I never received an answer. So I knew I was in danger. That's why I took my ten members. In my statements, I say I was -- my family was composed of ten persons, and we left in the direction of Pristina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Aliu, do you understand -- do you understand Serb?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So what you're referring to is that the Serb police, they are communicating in Serbian, but they referred to the names of cities in some code name. So that's what you understood; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. They used the code for Prishtina when they gave the order to the police stations. It was -- the order was that the whole population should be ousted from the villages and sent in the direction of Prishtina. They used the code in the case of the town Prishtina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Please continue, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You said, a moment ago, that when you listened in to the conversation, you concluded that your family was in danger. And in the next sentence and in the same context, you said that you also concluded, as I say, that your family was in jeopardy because your house had previously been the target of some attacks. Now, my question to you is the following: Did you conclude this from what you had heard in that conversation, that your family was in jeopardy, or did you conclude this, as you explained a moment ago, that you concluded your family was in jeopardy because your house had been the subject of attack on previous occasions? Which of the two is correct?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET ALIU
utterances.text: I'm not clear about the question, I'm afraid. I think I was clear in my explanation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, it will be easier for the witnesses, and we will save time and you will save time, if you don't repeat to the witness the answer which he's given. Just ask the witness the next question. People often do that in cross-examination, repeat the answers, but it takes up time and it makes things confusing. So with that in mind, just ask him the question that you want him to answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You said, therefore, that your family was in jeopardy because your house had previously been the object of attacks on several occasions. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET ALIU
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What he said, as I recollect, was this: He said he heard the order given and came to the conclusion that his house was in danger, having heard the order, because on previous occasions it had been the subject of attack. Is that right, Mr. Aliu?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: So he heard the order, and because of his previous experience, he thought the house was likely to be attacked.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's right. THE ACCUSED [Interpretation] All right. That is your explanation, Mr. May, but not the witness's explanation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That's what the witness said. There's no point trying to confuse him with further questions.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am not trying to confuse him. I'm just trying to get an answer to my questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Who did you get these codes from, the codes you claim you had for Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. the talks, the conversations that the police were having?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET ALIU
utterances.text: We were a professional army. We had members from all walks of life and professions, and just like all the other armies, we could get hold of these codes and were capable of leading these attacks in self-defence and doing all these things. We were not what you might think, just a crowd, a mob of people. We had a whole hierarchy of people there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So that's what you say about yourself. I did not say that; you said it about yourself. Now, if you knew the codes, tell me, then: What codes were there for Podujevo, Vucitrn, Suva Reka, Lapastica, et cetera? Which codes were they? What were the codes?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET ALIU
utterances.text: It was four or five years ago. I don't think I can remember the codes now, because the codes kept changing every week, every day sometimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What you're claiming didn't happen four or five years ago; it happened three years ago, what you're claiming took place.

utterances.speaker: MEHMET ALIU
utterances.text: It was -- it happened during 1988 and 1989. Sorry, 1998, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you mean that you heard, in 1998, how the chief issued orders to displace the Albanian population, to expel them from Kosovo Polje, Obilic, the village of Krusevo and Orlovac, which are the ones you mention?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET ALIU
utterances.text: It was in March 1999, not in 1998. It was in March 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Let it be 1999. Even then, those citizens were not expelled from those places. How, then, do you link up the order with the fact that this never took place?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's not a matter for the witness. He's given his evidence about what happened. You can make comments, if you want, in due course, but this is what he said happened.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He didn't say what happened; he said what he said. And what he said did not happen, did not take place, and that's the whole point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll hear evidence about that in due course. Now, can we go back to the witness's evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you don't know any of the codes for which you claim you used and which were subject to change, as you yourself said?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He says he doesn't remember. That is what he says.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, a pupil says the same thing when he doesn't know the answer to a question. I don't know whether the teacher then makes the distinction of whether he doesn't remember or doesn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, tell me: What activities, as the KLA, did you undertake in the Pristina area up until 1998?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET ALIU
utterances.text: I'm not clear about your question, I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You were a member of the KLA. Now, I'm asking you: What activities did your KLA organisation have in the area of Pristina up until 1998, or 1998 as well, included?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET ALIU
utterances.text: It didn't undertake any actions in the Prishtina area, in fact, in none of the cities, because it didn't want to put the population in danger. But the KLA was stationed in the mountainous areas in order not to bring any danger to the population, up to when it launched the offensive in -- when the offensive of Kacanoll was undertaken and the population asked for its assistance and the KLA went to the succor of the population.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So up until then, the KLA had no activities whatsoever; is that what you're saying? Have I understood you correctly?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET ALIU
utterances.text: What do you mean by "activities"?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The purpose for your organisation and establishment as the KLA. Why did you organise yourselves? Why did you set up the KLA?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET ALIU
utterances.text: We founded the KLA and started an uprising against the occupying Serbian forces. That's why we formed it. And for self-defence in our own country.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, what you've just said: "Started an uprising against the Serb forces." What activities? So this action is what I mean when I say "activities." What were those activities? What was that action that you took?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET ALIU
utterances.text: The action that the KLA took was called an uprising, and we started mobilising everything that was necessary from the massacre of the Jashari family. And before that, we were underground, but following the massacre at Qirez and the massacre of the Jashari family, the population had to defend themselves, so they rose in an uprising.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter requests the witness to draw closer to the microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Just give me short answers to my questions, please, to save time. Who was your KLA commander?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET ALIU
utterances.text: Rrustem Mustafa, with the nom de guerre of Remi, was my commander in the KLA. He led the Llap operational zone.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Where did you hold your meetings?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET ALIU
utterances.text: We held our meetings at the headquarters, where we had our place at Kacanoll, at the school.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How did you recruit new members?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET ALIU
utterances.text: Like all other armies. We did the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that you recruited them forcibly, individual members of the Albanian ethnic group?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET ALIU
utterances.text: We didn't have the right circumstances to recruit people. People came in as volunteers, and there were even only sons who agreed to join the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. So you're saying that it was on a voluntary basis. How was the KLA financed?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET ALIU
utterances.text: By the people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That's a very general answer. Did you personally finance the KLA?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET ALIU
utterances.text: Yes, with large sums, with everything that I could.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know any other way in which it was financed?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET ALIU
