utterances.text: Yes. It was also financed by Albanian women, who gave their own gold, their jewellery, and gave it to the KLA, saying, "Take my gold until Kosova is liberated." There have been cases when people -- when people married, they didn't hold a proper wedding, they didn't buy furniture, but they gave this money to the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, as you dealt in logistics, do you know any funds coming in from Germany, Switzerland, and so on?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET ALIU
utterances.text: Yes. Both aid and people came from Albanians who were emigrants there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And how did the money come into the country?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET ALIU
utterances.text: Very easily. When there's no lack of willpower, where there's a will, there is a way.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But I'm asking you specifically. What routes did the money come in by?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET ALIU
utterances.text: Well, I can tell you. I myself was in Hungary, and I brought aid by car through Serbia to Kosova on the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Including money?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET ALIU
utterances.text: Yes, money. Hard currency.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what weapons did your unit within the KLA dispose of?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET ALIU
utterances.text: All the kinds of weaponry that the police and army of your regime had that is the light weapons, we had them. And a large proportion was actually supplied by the police and army of your regime.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How were you supplied by weapons? As far as I was able to understand, you got your weapons from our police and army. Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET ALIU
utterances.text: We bought them with money.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you're saying that you purchased weapons from the army and the police. Is that it?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET ALIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, our police force didn't have any ammunition and weapons made in China. How were you then able to purchase these from them?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET ALIU
utterances.text: It seems that you're not listening to me. I said 80 per cent of our weapons came from the police and the army, and I can produce evidence of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I'd like to see that. And how did you finance the procurement of weapons?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET ALIU
utterances.text: With hard currency.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In the way in which you described a moment ago; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET ALIU
utterances.text: How do you mean? We bought weapons in Podujeva and in Prishtina. They brought them to Rudar and Medvedja by truck. They came to Peje and Kragujevc, and then we waited a week until they rubbed out the serial numbers and then we acquired them. I can produce evidence of this. Some of the weapons come from the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And who were these people who sold you the weapons?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET ALIU
utterances.text: They were members of your police and army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, can you tell me which members of the police and army who -- who were they who sold you the weapons?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET ALIU
utterances.text: One -- one of them was a member of Arkan's men, and he brought a truck full of weapons as far as Rudar. The truck was full of weapons, and then we met in the hotel in Rudar, and then we had a long conversation about your position.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I did not understand the answer. You had a long conversation about what position?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET ALIU
utterances.text: About your position personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: My personal position?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET ALIU
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: This is a conversation that you had with this man who was selling weapons to you. What was the name of this man?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET ALIU
utterances.text: For security reasons, they didn't tell their names because they were Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what did this conversation pertain to, the conversation you were having with him?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET ALIU
utterances.text: If the Court allows me, I can explain the entire conversation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Briefly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The weapons came, and we had an appointment in Rudar. We waited in the cafe until they arrived. And on that same day, President Milosevic and President Rugova, they asked us what we thought of them. Anybody -- they said, "We don't give a shit for Milosevic and Rugova. For us it's important to make money, because they have taken good care of their own families and are giving a hard time to our families. They are killing people for no reason." And they said that Arkan will do short work of Milosevic and will replace him in the long-run. That was the crux of the conversation. It was longer, of course, but it took two hours. It will take me several days to tell you every and each of the words we said. After they left, they -- the police didn't stop them. They escorted us up to Stedine village where the truck was waiting. There was also 5.000 metres of cloth for uniforms. There were some mortars, 12.7 millimetres; and a large quantity of bullets, 35.000 Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. bullets; 100 sniper rifles; Kalashnikovs. They escorted me up to the place and then I took them to our position in Kacanoll.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How many of them were there?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET ALIU
utterances.text: Four. There was a driver with a truck. There was another person. And I was accompanied with three other people. We had our car, and no police, roadblocks, check blocks gave us any hard time because those Serbs had the proper authorisation, and nobody dared stop them on the way.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And it is your assertion that these were some of Arkan's men?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET ALIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: On the basis of what you talked to with them, was it your conclusion that they were with him or against him?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET ALIU
utterances.text: They were with Arkan, against yourself. They said that the only person important in Serbia is Arkan, who keeps his family in Serbia, who fights with his family, whereas the others stay in power while their families are in safe places abroad.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So they were on his side against me. That is your assertion.

utterances.speaker: MEHMET ALIU
utterances.text: That was their assertion, not mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, do you know that my family was in Yugoslavia throughout and that they were not anywhere abroad?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We're getting far from the indictment now.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He's talking about an assertion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. He's describing a conversation. Now, let's move on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I doubt that explanation, but we can go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Were you personally issued with some kind of a weapon? Did you have a personal weapon of your own?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET ALIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What kind of weapon did you have?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET ALIU
utterances.text: Up to the time I was engaged in supplying, in logistics, I didn't need a weapon. I just had a stick, a baton. But when I joined the army after the NATO airstrikes again and your army started their attacks, I also got a weapon. I had a Skorpion.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter corrects herself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What kind of weapon did you have exactly?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET ALIU
utterances.text: You are asking me to tell you what weapon I had?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MEHMET ALIU
utterances.text: It is my own personal secret.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Where were KLA members trained for using weapons?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET ALIU
utterances.text: We had our own training sites, shooting ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How many terrorist actions did you take in the territory of Pristina and in the surrounding area?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET ALIU
utterances.text: You might wish to call them terrorists, but I don't agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm not asking you about qualifications. I'm asking you about how much you did in the territory of Pristina.

utterances.speaker: MEHMET ALIU
utterances.text: This is not something that I should answer. Somebody else can answer this question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Why can't you answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because I didn't take part in this kind of thing. I don't know about this kind of operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I raise a matter? This is plainly important evidence as far as the accused is concerned for issues involved within his defence. If this witness is able to help with information that he knew, having been an insider within the KLA, it would be extremely helpful for the accused if those answers were to be given, and in those circumstances, the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He's given an answer about the last question. He says he doesn't know about it. Yes. There's also the matter of time. The hour which the accused is usually given in cross-examination is now up. Would you apply for a longer time in this particular case, Mr. Kay?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Certainly. I was going to ask for a far longer period than normal, in view of the evidence this witness can give as well as the conciseness of the accused's questioning, which obviously is of importance when he is questioning witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. We'll consider that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, we will extend the time. Mr. Milosevic, we expect you to finish by 1.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Before I continue, could you please tell me when this event occurred exactly, the event you just described, when you bought a truckload of weapons from these persons, from those four men you mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MEHMET ALIU
utterances.text: This was about January, February - I don't remember exactly - in 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In January or February 1999?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET ALIU
utterances.text: I don't remember exactly, because I was on a lot of tours, and I don't remember which one. I also have the fax to bring the shipment to Medvedja.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And did you make this institution aware of that fax? We can go on. Do you know how many armed persons the KLA had in 1998?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET ALIU
utterances.text: No. It was not for me to know. My job was merely to supply food.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: If you say no, let's just save time. You say that it was only up to you to supply them with food; right?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET ALIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: A little while ago you said that you supplied them with weapons as well.

utterances.speaker: MEHMET ALIU
utterances.text: Everything: weapons, food, vehicles, and whatever I could, whatever kind of goods I could buy for the KLA. Whenever I had the opportunity, I bought things and sent them, as did all of my group. For instance, there was Ahmed Ajeti, who was a mechanic in Podujeva, and he worked as a mechanic servicing your vehicles, and they sent him weapons, saying that we were sending him vehicles. And that was one supply route. And round about 1992, when the war in Croatia started, I had my own business, and they asked me -- people who wanted to desert from the army when the war in Croatia started, they -- and I sent them civilian clothes. And they left their weapons there, and I collected those weapons and used them. That was in 1992, 1993, during the war in Bosnia. There was only one case in which there were 11 desertees who came with their weapons, and I gave them aid --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ryneveld.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Your Honour, I realise this is highly unusual, but a highly unusual situation has just arisen. The witness has been asked about documentation about this particular matter, about the selling of arms, et cetera, et cetera. Not included in his statement, not included in the attachments, the witness has brought a document with him to this session which is provided to us, which is not properly something that we could submit as far as the 92 bis. Normally I would re-examine on this document, but perhaps it is important that this document get distributed so that the accused has an opportunity to deal with the matter, since it's arisen during cross-examination. I just thought I should bring this to the attention of the Court and the accused, in fairness to everyone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Because if I were to wait until re-examination, I wonder whether that would be appropriate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let's put it on the ELMO and we'll have a look at it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Again, I'm unable to assist in terms of what it says, but I know it relates to the subject matter presently under discussion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Aliu, would you look at that. Is that the document you were referring to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It says here: [As read] "12.7" - that's a machine-gun calibre - "can be provided, three pieces. Price, 2.000 Deutschmark." Then it says: "Both types of rifles" - I don't know what this refers to - "for the time being, 100 pieces, according to the agreed price." And then it says: "Munitions for a 12.7-millimetre machine-gun, about 30.000 pieces, two Deutschmarks per piece. Munitions" - this is a bit deleted - "for rifles, 7.62 millimetres, will be prepared, about 150.000 pieces. According to plan, these major goods will be taken care of by the end of the month because all of this cannot be obtained and placed in a safe place and cannot be carried out before additional activity on a truck for transportation." And then there's something deleted. I can't see this. This seems illegible. I can't see whether it says "Malisheva" or "Mitrovica," but in the original you can probably see what it says. It starts with a capital letter, so I assume that it is the name of a town. So "That version is acceptable," it says. And then it says: "For you personally, you will get a gift, a Heckler, 9 millimetres, automatic." Could you please lift the page further up. A bit further up. A bit more. "It should only be confirmed, as soon as possible, in order to have yet another shipment taken care of. Plastic explosives and those ignition fuses." I can't read this. Could you please put it up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "Main" I can't read this. "The main," and there's another word. "At least 80 kilogrammes, and then 100 kilogrammes. Agrees to return to warehouse so that then all these other goods could be paid for in a deferred way" - I imagine he's referring to deferred payments - "for transportation by truck. I would have to" - I can't see this properly on this monitor - "get this"? "Get this"? He mentions a telegram. "When I tell you that we should talk." Sunday. It says "on Sunday" up here. Sunday, telegram. "This Sunday we should talk." And that's the end of this page.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So this is your communication in writing, with your provider of weapons; right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let's go over the page to see -- is there a second page? No. That's it. Thank you very much. Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: At any rate, most of it is legible. On the original, you can probably see those words that are illegible this way. Who sent you this? Are these the same people who actually sold this to you?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET ALIU
utterances.text: No. Other people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Who are these other people who provided you with explosives, machine-guns, rifles, et cetera? Who sent you this paper, these people that you were cooperating with? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MEHMET ALIU
utterances.text: Yes. It's not "as far as Malisheva" that's written there, but "Medvedja," "as far as Medvedja." That's what's written there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I see. Up to Medvedja. All right. That can be established when it's read precisely. That's no problem. It seems a bit blurred, especially on this screen. So who are these people?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET ALIU
utterances.text: They are -- for security reasons, these are people in Serbia, so I can't say who they are, but this is to show that we were supplied by your people, and that's the evidence that I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Your Honours, in fairness, this document having been read into evidence, might it be marked as an exhibit?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, and it can be translated in due course.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Yes. The other thing I should note is that it appears to be a fax with a date of March 20th, 1999, which is barely legible, would not show up, but that is the top right-hand corner on the fax.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Let it be exhibited, let it have a number, and let the accused see it. If you exhibit it --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. It will be Exhibit 116.1 ter.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, you can see now that it says "Medvedja," because on the screen it could not be read. That's right. It says, "Medvedja," 20th of March, 1999, at 20 past 11.00, judging by the fax. Yes. Oh, I thought this was an original. This is a fax. But obviously you know who you were communicating with.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is that right or is that not right?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Usher. You can take this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Did you know who it came from, is the question.

utterances.speaker: MEHMET ALIU
utterances.text: Yes, we knew from the people who supplied us, but the names are --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter asks the witness to move closer to the microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So that means that you can identify the perpetrators of this crime?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He said that for security reasons he does not want to give the names, and I, for one, would support that answer.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but he is duty-bound to give those names.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Not necessarily. We'll discuss it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Kay. What is the evidential value anyway?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If it is of evidential value, and it may be, perhaps the names could be written down on a piece of paper, kept under seal, disclosed to the accused in the usual way, and then he may reflect upon whether he needs to use the names or not and the names can be protected.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I think I would need to be assured of the evidential value, because there is a clear possibility of prejudice.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It may be contrary to the interests of these individuals, but it may be prejudicial to the defence of the accused if he doesn't have the information, which is why I suggest perhaps it can go under seal, which means that it's a document that's protected from the public eyes, and it can be considered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What evidential value could it have? It could put them in danger. That's the point.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: As yet, I don't know, we don't know, because we don't know if the names are of any significance or not, but if the information is kept in a protected form - this Court is well used to dealing with protections for the Prosecution in relation to information in their case. In our submission, the same criteria should be applied to the accused. I don't know the names. No one else does except for this particular witness. So the significance of the issue can't be determined.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ryneveld.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Your Honours, I too cannot see the evidential value. The only reason I've brought the matter to the attention is that he was being cross-examined about whether there was any documentation. I felt I was duty-bound to bring it to the Court's attention. Having said that, in our submission, the names of the people who supplied it are totally irrelevant to the issue that it confirms the fact that the witness said that there is corroborative evidence of his testimony. That, clearly, is the issue. To put unknown persons at risk or at danger for disclosing this information, to me, with the greatest of respect, would not serve any useful purpose. If the Court is disposed to adopt the procedure suggested by Mr. Kay, I would ask that any discussion of this matter be in closed session and under seal, but that would be only secondary to my primary submission, that it can be of no assistance to the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, you've heard what's said. It's irrelevant in any event. What relevance can it have?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] How wouldn't the names of these criminals be relevant? If what the witness is saying is true, how then would the names not be relevant of criminals supplying a terrorist with weapons? They are very relevant, highly relevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No, to these proceedings, to this trial and the issues in it. That's the point.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I assume that you deal with crimes on the territory of Yugoslavia. That's at least what you claim. Now, if supplies of weapons to terrorist organisations is something that you consider to be legal, then I don't know what I can explain here. A whole series of crimes starts there. And probably theft and the illegal possession of weapons on all counts. And then ammunition, explosives, and other devices sowing death, they were sold to a terrorist organisation in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, we deal with crimes, yes, but here we are concerned with the crimes charged in the indictment. We are not dealing with crimes generally, crimes that were committed in Yugoslavia. And what you were asked to do was to demonstrate the relevance that this particular piece of evidence would have to an issue that has arisen in the trial. As far as I am concerned, you haven't -- you have not been able to demonstrate that relevance. On the other hand, there is a clear prejudice to the persons who gave that information, and that is what the Chamber has to consider as well.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But is not -- is it not clear that those individuals were accomplices in the execution of terrorist attacks, killings, explosions? You can see here that they're purchasing 80 kilogrammes of explosives, and you know that they planted explosives in marketplaces, bus stations, shops, coffee bars, et cetera. So is this not a case of accomplices in killings that arose from the activities of this terrorist organisation, a member of which the witness is?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We shall not require the witness to answer. Since it's an important issue and I think the first time it's arisen in these proceedings, we will explain why. The Court has a power to protect those who may be put in danger because of answers which are given. If there are matters which are of significance in a trial which require answers to be given, the Court can also require that they be given and afford some measure of protection, as the amicus has suggested. However, before the matter can even be considered, there has to be demonstrated some relevance in the particular proceedings, of the answer. In this case, the answer is, in our judgement, of no relevance at all. The significance of the witness's evidence is the way in which weapons were obtained. He's described that, and he's produced a document which supports his evidence on that count in that he was being supplied in the way which he said. Who individually was doing the supplying is a matter of no relevance at all. In any event, even if it was, the fact that the suppliers, if the identity of the suppliers were given, that their security, their safety would be put in danger would be sufficient for us to rule that the identity should not be given. So we will not require the witness to answer the question. Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please. I think you should bear in mind my claim that in support of the KLA terrorist organisation, we see the participation of the Secret Services of a whole series of countries. The names of those people who supplied them with weapons --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We have -- we have ruled on this issue, and there will be no further argument on it. Now, have you got any more questions for this witness?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a lot more questions, and I'll try to get through as many of them as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that in Pristina and the surrounding areas in 1998 there was an increased number of explosions in public places planted by the KLA? Just give me a yes or no answer, please, so that we can make the best use of our time.

utterances.speaker: MEHMET ALIU
utterances.text: It's not clear to me what he's asking. What does this question mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I asked you whether you know that in the town in Pristina and the surrounding areas in the course of 1998 a number of explosions were planted in public places by the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MEHMET ALIU
utterances.text: I don't know about this. And it's not true that they were placed by -- they were placed by your police forces and the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you say it's not true. All right, then. How many people lost their lives in those terrorist operations, the planting of bombs in Pristina and its environs? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET ALIU
utterances.text: We know that in terrorist operations carried out by the Serbian police and army, we know about these. But about any others, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. I could have assumed that your answer would be what it was. That's why you used -- you purchased the weapons, so as not to use them. Is that right? Is that how I'm to understand you? From the environs of Podujevo later on --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters apologise, but there is too much interference with the channels. We're unable to hear the accused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: They're having trouble with the interpretation. I'll ask the Registry to do something about the channels. There's supposed to be interference on the various channels.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We're hearing the Albanian interpretation on the B/C/S channel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The interpreters say they are hearing Albanian on the B/C/S channel.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: While we are waiting -- while we're waiting, Your Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Honours, it might be appropriate for me to raise a matter of the interpretation which has been brought to my attention during the course of the day. It concerns the Albanian translation of various questions that were put this morning. I'm not a speaker of either B/C/S or Albanian, as the Court knows, but that various matters were raised with me, and I've had a chance to review the transcript to assess how a witness seems not to be understanding questions that were put, that there appear to have been no linkage between questions and answers. It may be appropriate that the transcript of today's proceedings be checked by the translation services to see if there were any problems in what was being relayed over the Albanian channel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It may have been the nature of the questions, but we'll do that. We will have it done. We'll go on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I ask something, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- question for the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm told it should be all right. Yes, Mr. Aliu.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a question for the Chamber. May I pose the question, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Not usually, but what is it?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET ALIU
utterances.text: The term used by Milosevic in relevance to me, calling me "terrorist," that's not appropriate. I'm here in the position of a witness. He's there in the position of accused. It's not appropriate to exchange such terms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He is entitled to ask questions within limits. We bear in mind what he said, and we bear in mind what you say. Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you went home with ten people, ten soldiers of the KLA. How big is your yard?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET ALIU
utterances.text: I went home with ten members of my own family who were in the town. My yard is about 40 acres, and it is surrounded by a wall of about three metres high.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you mean 40 acres or 40 R's, or could you give me a figure in hectares, please?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET ALIU
utterances.text: Two hectares.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Two hectares, you say. Is there a fence round your yard?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET ALIU
utterances.text: It is a wall made of strong material that surrounds my yard.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So there's a wall made of strong material around your yard. Now, how high is that wall?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET ALIU
utterances.text: About three metres. Even -- some places higher, some places lower.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That means that your yard, surrounded with this wall which is three metres high, was that made to be a fortification or was it the yard and the courtyard to your property, with a fence?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET ALIU
utterances.text: It is my own right to do what I want with my property, to build what I wish there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm not questioning your right to build. I'm just asking you that when you say a strong wall three metres high, I'm just asking you is that a yard or is it a fortification? What did you want to build?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET ALIU
utterances.text: It is a yard, and it's my personal property, I said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Were you trying to fortify it or not? That's the point that's made.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I didn't want to fortify it. But it is our tradition to surround our yards. Not only myself but all Albanians that can afford to do that build surrounding walls. It's an old tradition of ours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's what I was saying, precisely that, on other occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So how, then, can you say that there were 10.000 people in your yard when you say that the yard is two hectares in surface area?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET ALIU
utterances.text: It was possible to have even a larger number of people in smaller areas, because in that place, about 3.600 students had their lessons there. In Prishtina school of economics, for example, studied 1.500 students. So a total of 3.500 students had their lessons there in that compound, let alone talking about refugees who were panic-stricken. They could stay there, herded there, even 100.000 of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I was just asking you that. Two hectares is 100 metres times 200 metres, roughly. That's clear. One hundred metres times 200 metres. That's the rough surface area. Now, on that area, there are buildings there too, so it's not an empty place this space, this 100 by 200. And you claim that there were that many people there. Just yes or no. One hundred thousand.

utterances.speaker: MEHMET ALIU
utterances.text: I already said I couldn't count them one by one, but I said about 10.000 people who were driven out of Bardh i Madhe village, Fushe Kosove, and on a critical day, even from Dragodan.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. You said that on the 28th of March, you and some of your associates or family members or KLA soldiers, it doesn't matter any longer, that you slept in a shelter not far from your home. Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: MEHMET ALIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was that a dug-in shelter of any kind?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET ALIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what was it made out of, built of?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET ALIU
utterances.text: It was a hole dug in the ground. It was -- a hole was built and it was disguised, which the Serb forces, paramilitaries, they stayed there. And it was a very well-disguised place. Nobody could detect it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. I'll skip a few of my questions because I see I just have 11 more minutes. It's 11 to one. Describing the clash with the police which you led from your house on the 31st of March, 1999, did you throw hand grenades at the police on that occasion? And judging by what you said, you killed six policemen. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET ALIU
utterances.text: It is not correct. We didn't see them with our own eyes because some iron doors prevented them -- us. But when they came near, they shouted in Serbian, "Open up your doors. Fuck your mothers." And they shot in our direction, and we shot back, and that was it. We saw them when they executed 13 people. This is something we saw with our own eyes, not only myself but many other people who were there. I could tell you -- I could show you the place where that occurred.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you something else. How many policemen did you kill then?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET ALIU
utterances.text: Five or six remained killed, as the witness said. Of course you may have more precise figures because you were well-informed, certainly, being their chairman.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I am asking you. How many of them did you personally kill?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET ALIU
utterances.text: I said it very clearly. Personally, I didn't kill them. We were protecting ourselves. I know that we fired back in response to their firing, and some people got killed in the process. I can't tell you how many. You may have a more precise figure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm looking at your facts and figures. You said you threw bombs, grenades. Now you say that five or six got killed, and I'm asking you how many you personally killed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He has answered that. We can also read what's in the statement in which he said: "We responded with return fire and threw a number of hand grenades. I think about five or six of the police were killed." Now, that's his account in the statement, and he's given his answers about it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How many people took part on your side in that clash with the police in what you refer to as an exchange of fire, or, "We responded with return fire"?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET ALIU
utterances.text: I couldn't count them because there were rank and file people who were there. I can't give you an exact figure. There were many people. We were afraid. I have stated in my statement we were afraid because there were about 300 women and children, and we were afraid for them lest the Serb forces came and assaulted them. There were children, women from my family, from other families. So we didn't have time to think who was there but just to think what we would do in self-defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. So on your side, on the KLA side, many people took part in that clash, as you say. You didn't count them, but you said many; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET ALIU
utterances.text: I didn't say there were many there in that particular place, but there were many round about. I was with my own family members and people were killed even while they were on board the trucks. They stopped at the cemetery and they executed them. They stopped them when they were at the tiles factory and executed some of them. So -- many things were happening at the same time one couldn't follow up everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me this: San Giovanni, who came to you, was he an Albanian by origin?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET ALIU
utterances.text: Who is this San Giovanni? Please be more explicit in your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you about an individual whom I assume organised the visit of the Italian parliamentarians to your house.

utterances.speaker: MEHMET ALIU
utterances.text: It happened during the time when we were having the education there. It was not only that group. Many groups came there. There was also the wife of Zimmerman who visited the schools.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what about Christopher Hill, the US ambassador? When did he visit you?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET ALIU
utterances.text: I don't remember the date. I can't keep track of all the dates.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did he come once or several times?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET ALIU
utterances.text: Personally, I've seen him only once. He has come and visited the school. You can ask him yourself. I know that he visited that home school, and your police came and saw also the OSCE representatives coming there. I have stated that in my deposition.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And you said that you were also visited by the wife of US Ambassador Zimmerman, that she came to your house too. That was at the beginning of the 1990s.

utterances.speaker: MEHMET ALIU
utterances.text: She did not come to my home but to that home school, because I used to live in another home when I gave one of my homes to be used as a school. The murder of the school principal and the owner was something that all knew about.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So the school was the reason that they came, but I assume you met them.

utterances.speaker: MEHMET ALIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, when you met them, during these meetings, was there anybody else, any other prominent representatives of the KLA or the political life of the area, or Albanian political parties, or any other public officials, personages?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET ALIU
utterances.text: I kindly ask the Chamber to recall that I haven't stated they visited me. I have said that they visited the school. So you can find --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We take that. You were asked if there were other Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. prominent representatives present or not. If you can remember. If you can't remember, just say so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't remember. They didn't visit me, I said. They visited the school.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but you would see them - you said that a moment ago - when they visited the school. Did they know -- did you tell them that you were a member of the KLA?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET ALIU
utterances.text: You must have forgotten that I never said that I met and talked to them. I clearly said that they visited the school, but not me. You can find the relevant documentation with the Human Rights Council. They didn't come to visit me, never. They visited the school, my home when it was used as a school, I mean, but not me personally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Anything else, Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you get any recognition for your activities in the KLA?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET ALIU
utterances.text: Yes. Not only me, but the entire Albanian people got recognition, because today they are free. In the past, they didn't dare leave their own yards, and today they are free. That is our remuneration.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's now 1.00. Very briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think the questioning of this witness is quite considerable, in view of his importance and his evidence. I'm looking at page 6 of his statement, paragraph 4, where there are issues there that remained untouched, and it may be far more appropriate for the accused, upon considering the matter with his advisors, may want to develop a strategy in relation --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. It's a question of time, though. This witness -- can this witness be here next Wednesday?

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Frankly, Your Honour, I hadn't anticipated him being here that long, so I haven't made that inquiry. Perhaps he could be asked personally whether -- I'm sorry. Without speaking to him, which I'm not allowed to do now -- I thought he would be done today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Well, everybody did, and matters have developed. Mr. Aliu, can you stay here until Wednesday? We're not sitting until then. Or can you come back perhaps at a convenient time to conclude your evidence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can come another time. I'm busy this time. I thought that I would be done today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. So did everybody else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, we've got to balance what's reasonable with the points you want to make. If there are further points you want to make, you can make them not through the witness, but directly to us. But if you would like ten minutes, you can have it now, and then we'll conclude.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I'll see what I can do, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Witness, I want to ask you some questions now about your activities during the conflict in Kosovo in 1999. Do you understand?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET ALIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You have made a statement, where you have said that, "Ten of us, along with twelve of the civilians who decided to join us, went to the hills and continued with our duties relating to the war." Do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET ALIU
utterances.text: Yes. This was after what happened in my home, and I had to leave my home because I knew that if the Serb forces found me there - and some people volunteered to join me, who wanted to join the army, the KLA, we took to the hills and did join the army - there was no way out for me, because I was sure that they had intercepted me somewhere. I knew what would happen to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: In which area were you joining the army?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET ALIU
utterances.text: In Llap area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And were you taking part in armed battles with the Yugoslav army or the police?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET ALIU
utterances.text: We didn't have a chance to engage in clashes because they were -- the army and the police were in large numbers and they drove out the population in a day and left in the direction of Hertica, Turucica. When we were staying in Turucica, through the radio link, we heard from our superiors that the commander of Llozhan station, called Zoran, had ordered his -- had informed his superior, telling them that we would make the waters of Batllava Slobova Lake red with the blood of the Albanians. Then we received orders to head the population in the direction of Prishtina to save them. We were dressed in civilian uniforms, and we were escorting the population when we were ordered to see them up to Koliq but no further, because we were in danger. Then, when they arrived in Makovc, the massacre of 100 people occurred; that is, I think about 360 people actually got killed there in that place.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I'm asking you questions only about what you did, and I'd like you to answer those questions rather than referring to any other matters, because we only have a short period of time. Do you understand?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET ALIU
utterances.text: We did nothing on our own. We just executed orders. I'm telling you what our commanders told us to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Let counsel ask the witness this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Were you in operations with people from your unit before the war started? Was it the same people you worked with?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET ALIU
utterances.text: I didn't understand you. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You told us that your job was that of logistics and that you had a commander.

utterances.speaker: MEHMET ALIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Were you operating with the same group of men or a different group of men?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET ALIU
utterances.text: The Llap area had only one commander, and we acted all under the same commander. We were many units. I don't know how you can understand that. We had Rrustem Mustafa, with the pseudonym Remi, as our commander, and he was that commander of Llap area. I was responsible for the logistics unit, the others were responsible for other units, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: How many units did you have?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET ALIU
utterances.text: We had many units. It was not my job to know how many units there were. I was quartermaster and I was responsible for providing supplies and I had my collaborators with whom I worked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You were in charge of logistics, so you should have a very good idea as to the number of units.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I was that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Can you help us with the number of units?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that we were one and the same unit. We were taking part in an uprising to liberate our people. I was doing my job in the logistics, and this is all I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Were there armed units?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET ALIU
utterances.text: You mean the logistics unit or the other units of the KLA?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Were there other units that were armed?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET ALIU
utterances.text: No. Only the KLA. There wasn't any other army. We didn't have tanks and aviations, but we were popular uprisings, having light weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: There were KLA units that had weapons that were conducting armed battles; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET ALIU
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, they were part of KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: As a logistics officer, were you supplying them with weapons during the battles?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET ALIU
utterances.text: We supplied them with weapons before the battles, because during the battles we couldn't do so. We could do nothing when they were fighting. We supplied them with weapons before the clashes. We didn't have much space to move around. There was only one area we had command of.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: How many people worked in your logistics unit?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET ALIU
utterances.text: About 20 people. Not only in the Llap area. We were responsible for the entire KLA, a total of 20 people.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The 20 people in the logistics, were they in different bases around Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET ALIU
utterances.text: We were civilians staying -- we couldn't go to cities and towns. I mean, we tried to disguise ourselves from the army and the police. We supplied the KLA with foodstuffs, with clothes and footwear, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You organised one area for a commander. Did the other logistics officers, the 20 of them, did they work to other commanders in the areas of Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET ALIU
utterances.text: Yes. They worked for the Drenica, Shala areas, and other areas. We used to supply all these areas. We were all involved in it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You've told us about receiving a shipment of arms. Were the other logistics officers performing the same tasks as you, receiving arms and distributing them?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET ALIU
utterances.text: Sir, we didn't have any ranks or anything. We were just a group trying to contribute as much as we could, whoever could lay hands on arms from the army, from the police. I supplied not only the Llap but for the entire staff, because if Llap area had weapons and the others couldn't, then how could the war be waged? So we systematically provided the KLA members, fighters, with weapons. We didn't have a very clear division of our responsibilities. We just provided -- for example, I provided weapons in Gllogjan once. Another time, someone from Gllogjan gave weapons to Llap. So this was how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And if the Court would permit me just one more matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It's out of context to this, but it arises from something I noticed in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You mentioned being involved as early as 1992, when the conflict was happening in Croatia. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET ALIU
utterances.text: I didn't say I was involved in the conflict in Croatia. I said that when the conflict broke out in Croatia - please follow me closely - when the conflict broke out, the Serb army, who was deployed in Prishtina, they were sent to the war, and the soldiers didn't want to fight in Croatia and in Bosnia, and they deserted. I used to know some Serb citizens who were from those areas, and they addressed me -- they called me on the phone, asking me to help them, their children, to take them outside the border. And there was a meeting place where we met, and I helped them. I felt it as an obligation, a human, moral, political obligation to help them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Ryneveld, there isn't time for re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. Sorry, Your Honour. I anticipated that, and although I have questions, I must forego them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Aliu, that concludes your evidence. Thank you for coming to the International Tribunal to give it. You are free to go. We'll adjourn until half past 9.00 Wednesday -- rather, 9.00, I think it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
